newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Ivory Coast sets debt-cutting plan with banks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ivory Coast sets debt-cutting plan with banks.

text.p: The Ivory Coast has reached agreement with the London Club of creditor banks on a plan allowing it to wipe out nearly a third of its $7.2 billion commercial debt, bankers announced on Friday.

The deal, in the form of a Brady-style debt restructuring plan, followed three days of talks in Paris and provides for elimination of a minimum 30 percent of the west African nation's commercial debt, said French bank Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP), which chaired the meeting.
"The principles of an agreement, which assumes the support of fund providers, were set forth for restructuring the Ivory Coast debt amounting to $7.2 billion," BNP said.
Some $4.6 billion of the debt stems from interest arrears accumulated since April 1987 when the Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, ceased payments.
The accord will allow the Ivory Coast "to restore the confidence of the international financial community in the country and thus, favour foreign investment," BNP said.

The agreement will pave the way for Ivory Coast to borrow again on the commercial market. But it appeared to fall far short of a call by Ivory Coast Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan earlier this month for a 75-percent debt write-off.
The two sides have been negotiating for the past two years, but talks were suspended in early October when they failed to reach common ground.

The Ivory Coast claimed to be a victim of its own economic success, with creditors pressing for a harder bargain based on a rebound in its economy since 1994. It was among Africa's top performing economies in 1995, notching up seven-percent growth. The Ivory Coast's total external debt is more than $15 billion.
Implementation of the deal with the steering committee of the creditor banks, which also include Chase Manhattan Bank, Citibank, Credit Lyonnais and Societe Generale, is targeted for mid-1997.
The debt talks were attended by a delegation from the Ivory Coast led by Finance Minister N'Goran Niamien.
The restructuring plan "takes account of the Ivory Coast's particular economic conditions" and involves a buyback, allowing elimination of a minimum 30 percent of the debt, BNP said.

For the remainder, two instruments would be issued at the discretion of the creditors -- a 30-year discount bond and a 20-year front-loaded interest-reduction par bond. There would also be a 20-year past-due interest bond.
The instruments would be issued in French francs and dollars according to the breakdown of the debt in the two currencies.
